newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr slips after RBA cuts rates.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr slips after RBA cuts rates.

text.p: The Australian dollar slipped in volatile morning trade after the Reserve Bank cut its official cash rate by 0.5 point to 5.0 percent.
The market has long been discounting such a move but the timing came as something of a surprise as most had expected the central bank to wait for its monthly board meeting next week.

Dealers felt the cut was largely priced in and expected US$0.7340 support to hold on the belief this was the last in the cycle. Indeed, after intitially falling to US$0.7395, the dollar had bounced to US$0.7415/20 by 9.35 am (2235 GMT), down on an early US$0.7455/60 but up on Tuesday's late US$0.7360/65.
The dollar had already enjoyed a sharp short covering rally overnight as buying from various sources, including a Swiss bank, U.S. funds and a Canadian corporate, triggered panic stop loss buying.
Dealers said it looked like many offshore investors had been very short of the currency having sold it aggressively since the last easing on May 23 when it had been trading up at 78 cents.

Much of the selling was in anticipation of another cut so the actual event ended up prompting profit taking on short positions. Where the dollar went from here depended crucially on how the market assessed the risk of yet another easing.

The market has been of the view the fifth move would be the last in the easing cycle -- which oddly enough began on Wednesday, July 31 last year -- and this belief was partly behind the dollar's resilience this morning.
But the RBA's statement on the move contained some bold assertions which had analysts wondering if the market was being too sanguine.
The bank noted that recent prices and wages data confirmed the absence of inflationary pressures in much of the economy and inflationary expectations in the community had taken a step lower.
Of particular note was the bank's comment that there was relatively little risk of encountering capacity constraints over the next year or two even if growth were stronger than expected.
"That is a very stong statement," said Tony Meer, an economist at Deutche Morgan Grenfell.
"Taken with its confidence that underlying inflation will remain under two percent into 1998, it suggests the bank sees enough room for yet another easing, if not two."
The market was not yet of that view, with the December 90-day bank bill contract up just 11 basis points at 95.06, implying a rate only a little below the 5.00 percent cash rate.
But speculation of a sixth cut could grow quickly should real side economic data, particularly on employment, fail to show the pick up so long anticipated by analysts.
That made next week's July labour figures even more important than usual and if they were to surprise on the downside, as they have for much of this year, the dollar could come under fresh pressure.

For now the dollar was showing great resilience having bounced back to US$0.7450, almost where it was before the cut was announced and dealers saw scope for further short covering toward US$0.7520 resistance.
On the crosses the currency held firm at 88.03/13 yen having rallied sharply offshore from 86.58/68 late here Tuesday and was broadly firmer on most other currencies as well.
Treasurer Peter Costello was quick to celebrate the good rate news, saying Australia now had a very good outlook in the coming year.
He thought the easing posed no danger to the dollar as it was justified by low inflation and well priced in to the market.
